title: Delegation of Authority and Approval Matrix
text: Approval authority is delegated by annual committed cost. Expenditure up to 10,000 EUR is approved by the team lead. Expenditure from 10,000 to 50,000 EUR is approved by the department director. Expenditure from 50,000 to 250,000 EUR requires the chief financial officer. Anything above 250,000 EUR requires executive committee approval. Approval authority may not be sub-delegated below the stated level and may not be split into smaller requests to stay under a threshold, which is treated as a governance breach. Multi-year commitments are assessed on total contract value, not on the annual figure.

title: Data Workflow Approval Procedure
text: Approval for a new data processing workflow is proportionate to its cost and scope. Data processing workflows under 25,000 EUR annual cost may be approved by the team lead alone, provided no special category data is involved. Workflows above that threshold are reviewed by the data governance working group at its monthly meeting. The requesting team documents the purpose, the data sources, and the expected output in the workflow intake form. Approval is recorded in the workflow register and is valid for twelve months.

title: Data Workflow Approval Procedure
text: All new data processing workflows require Data Governance Council sign-off regardless of cost. The cost-based exemption in the previous version of this procedure is withdrawn, because low-cost workflows were found to carry the same privacy risk as expensive ones. The council meets weekly and reviews the workflow intake form together with the data protection impact assessment screening result. Sign-off is recorded in the workflow register with the council decision reference. Workflows approved under the previous procedure remain valid until their next annual review, at which point they are reassessed under this procedure.

title: Procurement and Vendor Onboarding Process
text: Procurement proceeds through intake, assessment, negotiation, approval, and onboarding. Intake requires a business case stating the problem, the alternatives considered including build versus buy, and the expected benefit. Any vendor that will process company or customer data must clear security and privacy review before contract signature, and that review is a blocking gate rather than a parallel activity. Legal review is required for all contracts above 25,000 EUR and for any contract containing non-standard liability or indemnity terms. Purchase orders are raised only after approval; retrospective purchase orders require a documented exception.

title: Budget Planning and Variance Management
text: Budgets are planned annually with quarterly reforecasts. Teams submit headcount, vendor spend, and infrastructure cost separately so that cloud consumption can be tracked against committed discounts. A variance above ten percent against the quarterly forecast requires a written explanation to finance. Unspent budget does not carry over between fiscal years, which is deliberate: it removes the incentive to spend in the final quarter. New initiatives arising mid-year are funded through the contingency pool, which requires director approval and is capped at five percent of departmental budget.

title: Data Governance Council Charter
text: The Data Governance Council owns decision rights over data domains, data quality standards, and the approval of new data processing workflows. Membership comprises the chief data officer as chair, the data protection officer, the head of security, a finance representative, and the domain data owners. The council meets weekly and publishes decisions within two business days. Decisions are made by consensus; where consensus fails the chair decides and records the dissent. The council may delegate pre-approved patterns to teams, which is the preferred mechanism for reducing approval latency on routine work.

title: Platform Initiative RACI and Decision Rights
text: Every initiative names one accountable owner; shared accountability is not permitted because it reliably produces unowned work. Responsible parties execute, consulted parties must be asked before a decision is made, and informed parties are notified after. Product owns the problem statement and prioritisation, engineering owns the solution design and estimate, and security and privacy are consulted at design time rather than at release time. Escalation moves to the steering group when a consulted party formally objects and the objection cannot be resolved within five business days.

title: Business Case and Benefit Realisation Standard
text: A business case quantifies the expected benefit, the total cost of ownership over three years, and the payback period. Benefits are categorised as cost reduction, revenue growth, risk reduction, or capability building, and only the first two may be claimed as financial return. Estimates state their confidence level and the assumptions they depend on. Any initiative above 100,000 EUR total cost of ownership requires a benefit realisation review twelve months after delivery, comparing actual against forecast, and the result is reported to the investment committee irrespective of outcome.

title: Internal Service Level Agreements for Platform Services
text: Platform teams commit to published response times by request class. Production incidents are acknowledged within fifteen minutes during business hours and within thirty minutes outside them. Access requests are fulfilled within one business day. Architecture review slots are available within three business days. Security and privacy reviews are completed within five business days when the intake form is complete, and the clock pauses while information is outstanding, which is why incomplete submissions are the most common cause of perceived delay. Attainment against these commitments is published monthly.

title: Business Risk Acceptance Framework
text: Risk is accepted by the business owner, never by the engineering team implementing the control gap, because accepting risk is a commercial decision. Low risks are accepted by the department director, medium risks by the executive sponsor, and high risks by the risk committee. Every accepted risk records the exposure, the compensating controls, the review date, and an expiry no longer than twelve months. Accepted risks are reviewed quarterly and an expired acceptance reverts the item to an open finding automatically.

title: Organisational Change and Stakeholder Communication
text: A change that alters how people work is communicated before it is deployed, not alongside it. The communication names what changes, who is affected, when it takes effect, what action is required, and where to get help. Changes affecting more than fifty people require a named change champion in each affected team and a feedback channel monitored for two weeks after launch. Adoption is measured rather than assumed, with a target of seventy percent active usage within one quarter, and a shortfall triggers a review of the rollout rather than additional mandates.

title: Capacity and Headcount Request Process
text: Headcount requests are submitted in the quarterly planning cycle and are assessed against portfolio priority rather than team seniority. Each request states the outcome the role enables, the consequence of not filling it, and whether the work could be met by reprioritising existing capacity. Backfills are pre-approved within the agreed establishment. Contractor engagements above three months are treated as headcount for approval purposes to prevent permanent capacity being added outside the planning process. Approved roles that remain unfilled for two quarters return to the central pool.

title: Cloud Cost Allocation and Showback
text: Cloud cost is allocated to owning teams through mandatory resource tagging; untagged resources are charged to a shared overhead pool and reported as a tagging defect. Teams receive a monthly showback report with cost per service and cost per thousand requests, because absolute cost without a unit metric drives the wrong behaviour during growth. Commitment discounts are purchased centrally and the benefit is distributed proportionally to usage. A month-on-month cost increase above twenty percent triggers an automated review with the owning team.

title: Intake and Prioritisation for Platform Requests
text: All platform requests enter a single intake queue regardless of who asks, which prevents prioritisation by escalation volume. Each request is scored on reach, impact, confidence, and effort, and the score is visible to requesters. Requests that are genuinely urgent and important use the expedite lane, which is capped at two concurrent items so that expediting retains meaning. Requests that duplicate a roadmap item are merged and the requester is linked as a stakeholder. Anything unstarted after two quarters is closed with an explanation rather than left open indefinitely.

title: Build Versus Buy Decision Guidance
text: Buy when the capability is not differentiating and a mature market exists; build when the capability is core to competitive advantage or when integration cost exceeds licence cost. The comparison must include the full cost of building, which is dominated by ongoing maintenance rather than initial implementation, and the full cost of buying, which includes integration, data migration, and exit. Lock-in risk is assessed by asking how long replacement would take and what data would be recoverable. A hybrid path, buying the commodity layer and building the differentiating layer, is often correct and is frequently overlooked.

title: Management Reporting and KPI Standard
text: Each team publishes a small set of outcome metrics rather than activity counts, because activity metrics are easy to inflate and tell leadership little. Metrics are reported monthly with the trend and the target, and a metric without an owner is removed. Leading indicators are preferred where they exist. A metric that has not influenced a decision in two quarters is a candidate for retirement. Definitions are stored centrally so that the same metric name means the same thing in every report, which is the most common source of disagreement in review meetings.
